analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give workers 90 days' notice before mass layoffs or site closings, up from 60.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee in June 2022, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires many employers to warn workers 60 days before a mass layoff or plant closing. This bill would stretch that warning to 90 days, cover smaller employers than the current law does, close loopholes that let companies dodge liability through subsidiaries, contractors, or sales of the business, and add stronger penalties and a public database of layoff notices. It also lets workers' representatives and local governments sue to enforce the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers facing job loss from a closing or mass layoff, their unions, and the towns that depend on the affected employer. They would get three months' warning instead of two, notice that counts remote workers and sidesteps games with corporate structure, stronger back-pay remedies, and advance information about unemployment and retraining benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing layoffs and their communities

how_it_helps.text: Extends the required advance notice before a site closing or mass layoff from 60 to 90 calendar days, giving affected employees, unions, the governor, the state rapid-response agency, and local governments three months to plan.

Expands coverage to employers with 50 or more employees or a $2 million annual payroll, counts remote workers assigned to a closed site, and counts multiple small cutbacks in the same 90-day window as one mass layoff so they cannot be sliced below the notice threshold.

Pins liability on the parent, affiliate, or client company that actually made the layoff decision, not just the local entity, and makes sellers responsible for notice through the date of a business sale.

Adds liquidated damages equal to 30 days of back pay, a four-year deadline for lawsuits, a rule that workers cannot waive their rights in severance agreements without a private attorney or union representative, and requires employers to hand workers a guide to unemployment, COBRA, and retraining benefits.
Requires the Labor Department to run a public, searchable database of layoff notices and to notify the affected area's members of Congress within 15 days.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of significant size, which would bear the cost of three months of notice (often keeping payrolls and benefits running), face expanded definitions of who counts as the responsible 'employer,' and risk higher court judgments including liquidated damages. Workers whose jobs would have disappeared faster than 90 days under a shorter timeline could also see layoffs announced or structured differently.

drawbacks.text: A longer mandatory notice period is a real cost: employers must keep pay and benefits flowing for an extra month, and critics argue that during sudden downturns this can push firms to cut earlier or deeper to fit inside the notice window.

The bill reaches beyond the direct employer to any parent, affiliate, or client 'regardless of amount of ownership interest' that participated in layoff decisions, which could sweep in investors, franchisors, or customers with limited day-to-day control and generate litigation.

The narrow exception allowing an employer to shorten notice when early warning would scare off rescue financing or new business is fact-dependent, so disputes over whether a firm qualified would likely end up in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, three months of paid warning and better enforcement is a substantial benefit at a moment when losing a job without warning is devastating. The main honest cost falls on employers, who face about a month of added expense and broader legal exposure, and the expanded liability rules are written broadly enough that some lawsuits will target entities with only indirect control. On balance the bill's benefits to workers and communities outweigh its compliance costs, though the corporate-liability language is broader than strictly needed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on June 16, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the bill's last action; the committee never held a hearing, reported it, or brought it to a vote.
It drew only three cosponsors — two Senate Democrats and one Independent — and no version was introduced in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers benefit from the bill's death, since the current law's 60-day notice, narrower coverage, and looser liability rules stay in place; no member of the public gains.

industries.industry: Large and mid-size employers (50+ employees or $2M payroll)
industries.note: Under this bill they would owe workers 90 days of notice and pay instead of 60, and face easier lawsuits and added liquidated damages when they close or lay off. Workers and towns gain the warning the employers would rather not give.

industries.industry: Parent companies, franchisors, and clients of staffing firms
industries.note: The bill makes any parent, affiliate, or client that participates in layoff decisions liable for notice, regardless of how small its ownership stake is, closing a route companies currently use to shift layoff blame to a local entity.
Unions and worker representatives would receive direct notice of layoffs, gain standing to sue for violations, and control any waiver of workers' rights in settlements.
